research_text:
## Research brief

### 1. What the API and finding concern

`javax.net.ssl.SSLContext` represents a secure-socket protocol implementation. It supplies secure socket factories and `SSLEngine` instances and is initialized with key managers, trust managers, and a source of randomness. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html?utm_source=openai))

The supplied message, **“the observed call sequence is not one SSLContextSpec accepts,”** refers to the detector’s model of calls on a context—not directly to a TLS handshake or negotiated protocol. The published rule’s order is `Get, Init, Engine?`: a modeled factory call, then initialization, optionally followed by engine creation. The message alone does not identify the missing or out-of-order call. The rule also has separate forbidden-call, protocol-value, and required-predicate provisions; the message alone does not establish which of those, if any, also failed. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

### 2. Documented usage and remediation guidance

Oracle’s documentation describes two relevant usage paths:

- For a newly obtained context, call `init` before using it to create an engine or socket factory. The API documents an `IllegalStateException` for these operations if the implementation requires initialization and it has not occurred.
- `SSLContext.getDefault()` returns an immediately usable default context without requiring initialization. This is valid API usage even though the cited CrySL rule forbids that call. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html?utm_source=openai))

The API permits null arguments to `init`. Oracle’s JSSE guide specifically says that a null key-manager array defines an empty key manager, a null trust-manager array uses an appropriate manager obtained from an installed provider, and a null random argument uses a default implementation. An empty key manager is relevant if the application needs to present credentials. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html?utm_source=openai))

For safe use, Oracle documents that trust managers make peer-trust decisions and that applications using raw `SSLSocket` or `SSLEngine` must also verify the peer’s identity; raw sockets and engines do not automatically match a URL hostname against the peer credentials. The API also recommends explicitly setting an engine’s client or server mode. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html?source=:ow:lp:cpo::))

The official sources do **not** prescribe one universal remediation for every detector finding. Their documented guidance is to initialize a newly created context appropriately, use suitable authentication and trust configuration, and configure connection parameters as needed. They do not require replacing every `getDefault()` or `getInstance("TLS")` call merely because this particular CrySL rule rejects it. Oracle’s JSSE guide itself illustrates `getInstance("TLS")`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html?utm_source=openai))

### 3. Compatibility and migration

- **Protocol selection:** The CrySL whitelist tests the requested `getInstance` string. Oracle states that a context named `TLS`, `TLSv1.2`, or `TLSv1.3` may support other protocol versions too. Supported, enabled, and negotiated versions are distinct; neither the string `TLS` nor a rule violation establishes what was negotiated. Enabled protocols can be controlled separately on sockets or engines. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html?utm_source=openai))
- **Wire compatibility:** Oracle documents TLS 1.3 compatibility risks involving different cipher suites, certificate signature support, close behavior, session resumption, and key updates. It describes a backward-compatibility mode but does not promise that every peer or application will interoperate. Its guide also documents a close-notify property for a particular close-behavior migration issue. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html))
- **Platform support:** Java SE 17 requires `TLSv1.2` support for `SSLContext`; the Java SE 26 specification requires both `TLSv1.2` and `TLSv1.3`. Oracle documents TLS 1.3 in JDK 8u261 and later. Availability and enabled defaults still depend on the actual platform and provider. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))
- **Persisted formats:** The consulted `SSLContext` and JSSE sources do not document a general keystore or other persisted-format migration as a consequence of changing this call sequence. They do not establish compatibility for a particular application’s stored keys, certificates, or session state.

No source reviewed establishes a migration path that is appropriate for every finding. Protocol-policy and peer-compatibility evidence would be needed before pinning a versioned context.

### 4. Exact rule matching

The published file contains this matching and ordering clause, quoted verbatim: ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

```text
SPEC javax.net.ssl.SSLContext

EVENTS
	g1: getInstance(protocol);
	g2: getInstance(protocol, _);
	Get := g1 | g2;

	i1: init(km, tm, random);
	Init := i1;

	se1: eng = createSSLEngine();
	se2: eng = createSSLEngine(_,_);

	Engine := se1 | se2;

ORDER
	Get, Init, Engine?
```

The rule separately declares `getDefault() => Get` under `FORBIDDEN`; requires `protocol` to be exactly `"TLSv1.2"` or `"TLSv1.3"`; requires `generatedKeyManagers[km]`, `generatedTrustManagers[tm]`, and `randomized[random]`; and declares the two resulting predicates after `Init` and `Engine`, respectively. These are rule predicates, not evidence of certificate validation or a negotiated protocol. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

- The specified type is **`javax.net.ssl.SSLContext`**. `getInstance` and `getDefault` are static API methods; `init` and `createSSLEngine` are instance methods of that API.
- **Parameter lists are constrained:** the file names one- and two-argument `getInstance` patterns, a three-argument `init` pattern, zero- and two-argument `createSSLEngine` patterns, and zero-argument `getDefault`. The `_` entries do not name a value to be constrained; they do not mean an arbitrary number of parameters. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))
- **A method on an unrelated type does not match merely because it shares one of these names:** the rule is specified for `javax.net.ssl.SSLContext`, not as a name-only predicate over arbitrary receiver types. The file itself does not document every detector implementation detail concerning dispatch or subtype resolution. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

### Source limitations

The linked rule is on the mutable `master` branch. The supplied SHA-256 and the detector’s compiled rule artifact and version were not independently verified in this research pass. The rule file also does not explain a presentation-level diagnostic such as “unknown.”

**Primary source URLs**

- CrySL rule: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl
- Oracle `SSLContext` API: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html
- Oracle JSSE guide: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html
- Oracle standard algorithm names: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html
- CrySL authors’ language paper: https://drops.dagstuhl.de/storage/00lipics/lipics-vol109-ecoop2018/LIPIcs.ECOOP.2018.10/LIPIcs.ECOOP.2018.10.pdf
